source_read: PMC HTML PMC11374807, full text (abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion with limitations, author contributions and funding, data availability, competing interests). Fig. 1 (coefficients and significance) and Fig. 2 (LASSO ranks): a screenshot of my tab came back blank, so figure image not viewable; values printed only there were not used. Supplemental Material (Word file: Table S1, S4, Fig. S2 sensitivity analysis) not read.

claims.overstatement: (1) 'Bodies that differ (here the CYP2D6 enzyme) and earlier hallucinogen use are among the reasons people feel more or less from the same amount' is causal. For CYP2D6 a mechanism is stated by the authors (genotype, exposure, effect), but previous hallucinogen experience is a between-person association that could equally reflect who goes on using (or tolerance); 'are associated with' is what the source shows. (2) 'Lying in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present': the source says participants were mostly in a bed in such a room; some sessions included MRI scanning. (3) 'Lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6': the predictor is a genotype-based activity score (the abstract calls it genetically determined functionality); 'liver' is the editors' gloss. No dosing advice: the closing sentence correctly says that taking more after feeling little was not tested; the authors' own suggestions (mood enhancement with MDMA before a psychedelic, ascending doses, multiple sessions) are rightly left out.
claims.note: Part not supported by the text: 'the differences between women and men were not significant when one dose per study was analysed' (and the magnitude's parenthesis) is stated in the text only for the slightly less positive experience reported by women (Discussion, 1st paragraph); whether the smaller temperature change in women survived the one-dose sensitivity analysis is not in the text and could only come from Supplementary Fig. S2, not read. Everything else found as stated: 213 (108 women), 25 to 64 years; 9 studies, 8 with placebo; 297 LSD and 189 placebo sessions; single oral doses 25 to 200 micrograms (analytically 26 to 197); 19 x 29 = 551 tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction; dose strongest for all effects except body temperature in the mixed models, selected for all 29 in LASSO and largest for 21 (29 minus the 8 named exceptions = 21, recomputed). The abstract-results mismatch on sex and body weight is real. One more qualifier the claim could carry: in 2 of the 9 studies the 'dose' was back-estimated from the LSD plasma AUC, so the dose-plasma association is partly circular for those sessions.

anchors.locator: Methods and materials > Study design, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Pooled raw data from nine double-blind crossover studies at University Hospital Basel, 2014 to 2023, eight with placebo (study #8 had no placebo session), all registered; 213 healthy participants, 297 LSD-only sessions and 189 placebo sessions analysed (sessions combining LSD with another substance excluded).
213 healthy participants (108 female), aged 25 to 64 (mean 32, SD 9), recruited from the University of Basel campus; body weight 70 kg (SD 12; 50 to 104).

anchors.locator: Methods and materials > Study drug, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Single oral doses of 25, 50, 100 or 200 micrograms (capsules or ethanol drinking solution), as study conditions; analytically confirmed doses 26 to 197 micrograms; for the first two studies the actual dose was estimated from the LSD plasma AUC.

anchors.locator: Methods and materials > Predictor variables, Response variables and Statistical analyses (1st to 4th paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: 19 predictors: sex, age, dose, body weight, CYP2D6 genotype activity, number of previous hallucinogen experiences, MRI during the session, Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS) subscales rated before intake, NEO-FFI traits; no expectation measure. Responses as LSD minus placebo: VAS, 5D-ASC and MEQ30 as area under the effect curve 0 to 11.5 h, peak blood pressure, heart rate and temperature, plasma AUC. Linear mixed models with random subject intercepts, dose as covariate, z-scored variables; Benjamini-Hochberg across all tests; LASSO for ranking; sensitivity analysis with one dose per study (N = 213).

Dose (26 to 197 micrograms) was the strongest predictor of all LSD-induced effects except body temperature, which was predicted only by sex (smaller change in women) and pre-drug emotional excitability. CYP2D6 activity score was the only other predictor of plasma LSD and was negatively associated with the 5D-ASC total and anxious ego dissolution. MRI sessions: more impaired control and cognition. Age positively and body weight negatively associated with VAS 'bad drug effect'.

Female sex: smaller LSD-induced increases in VAS good drug effect, 5D-ASC experience of unity and insightfulness, MEQ30 positive mood. Previous hallucinogen experience: lower 5D-ASC total, anxious ego dissolution, vigilance reduction, disembodiment, impaired control and cognition, changed meaning of percepts, MEQ30 transcendence of time and space.

Pre-drug AMRS general well-being: second strongest predictor after dose, significantly associated with all subjective effects except VAS bad drug effect, 5D-ASC changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood (strongest with 5D-ASC total, VAS good drug effect, oceanic boundlessness). Activity, emotional excitability, (state) extraversion and anxiety predicted several subjective effects; excitability, inactivation and anxiety predicted heart rate; pre-drug anxiety predicted higher 5D-ASC anxiety; introversion predicted nothing.

Trait openness (NEO-FFI): higher 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness, spiritual experience, insightfulness, MEQ30 total, mystical and positive mood. Trait extraversion: higher 5D-ASC total, visionary restructuralization, auditory alteration, audio-visual synaesthesia. Neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness predicted no effect.

On average 12 predictors (8 to 14) selected per response; dose selected for all 29 and largest in 21; not top for VAS good drug effect, auditory alteration, vigilance reduction, spiritual experience, blissful state, MEQ30 mystical and positive mood, and body temperature; well-being top for good drug effect, vigilance reduction, spiritual experience, blissful state; openness top for mystical and positive mood; pre-drug anxiety second for 5D-ASC anxiety, heart rate and blood pressure.

Coefficient sizes and semi-partial R2 are given only in Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table S4; Fig. 1 legend: correction across 19 x 29 = 551 tests, N = 297. Figure image not viewable in my tab; supplement not read; the text gives no sizes.

Women reported a slightly less positive experience, not significant in the sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig. S2); older participants more bad drug effects; body weight and MRI smaller impact. Bad drug effects were generally small, smaller than good drug effects, and covered any negative state including nausea; anxious ego dissolution and anxiety were not associated with age; neuroticism had no pronounced influence.

Blinding is a known problem and expectations may influence effects (not measured); setting varied little: participants mostly in a bed in a quiet hospital room with one investigator, MRI the only setting predictor, music not controlled or assessed; lower CYP2D6 activity with more anxious ego dissolution is consistent with higher LSD concentrations; serotonin 2A receptor gene not studied; volunteers may be high in openness; linearity assumed (sensitivity and spline analyses said to agree).

Abstract and summary state that sex and body weight had no significant influence on the drug experience, although the Results report female sex with smaller increases in four subjective ratings and in temperature, and body weight with less VAS bad drug effect.
Authors speculate that improving mood before a psychedelic (for example with MDMA), multiple sessions, and ascending dose regimens might help; none of this was tested in these data.

claims.overstatement: None for the Vizeli sentence, which keeps to direction and significance and says the text gives no sizes. A qualifier worth adding: by the text, pre-drug well-being was significantly associated with every subjective scale except VAS bad drug effect, changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood, which includes the 5D-ASC anxious ego dissolution and anxiety scales, and the Discussion says effects were more pronounced with higher well-being (and also with higher pre-drug anxiety). In these laboratory data a better mood went with stronger effects generally, not with a less challenging session, so the Vizeli data do not illustrate the claim's opening generalization about a less challenging experience (the sign for those two scales is in Fig. 1, which was not viewable). 'Lying in a hospital room': mostly; 'just before the dose': the text says before drug intake.
claims.note: Numbers: 213 people, nine studies, eight with placebo (claim: 'mostly with a placebo session'): correct.

anchors.locator: Methods and materials > Study design, 1st paragraph; Subjects, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Nine Basel double-blind crossover studies, 8 of 9 placebo-controlled; 213 healthy participants; 297 LSD sessions.

Pre-drug AMRS well-being significantly associated with all subjective effects except VAS bad drug effect, 5D-ASC changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood; pre-drug AMRS anxiety predicted higher 5D-ASC anxiety; all adjusted for dose.
Trait openness predicted MEQ30 total and mystical scores and 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness, at a given dose.

Subjective effects were more pronounced with higher pre-drug well-being, extraversion, emotional excitability, activity or anxiety; setting varied little (mostly in a bed, quiet hospital room, one investigator).

key_findings.correction: Confirmed as worded (it lists only the four subjective ratings). Note: the text says only that the slightly less positive experience of women was not significant in the sensitivity analysis; it says nothing about the smaller temperature change in women there.

reporting_issues.note: Precision: the text states loss of significance in the sensitivity analysis only for the less positive experience reported by women (Discussion, 1st paragraph), not for the temperature difference; the card's 'only the sex findings are said to lose significance' slightly generalizes this.
Vizeli part confirmed (random intercept for subjects only). The comparison with Studerus et al. (2021) is checked in my studerus_2021 output.

Both secondary accounts checked in this session: Haijen 2018 Introduction (being psychologically well in the days before predicted peak experiences) and Aday 2021 Results (general psychological distress negatively related to oceanic boundlessness).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E for non-randomized between-person predictors is the right instrument despite the randomized source studies; overall some concerns fits an association question (dose-only adjustment, no study term, partly circular dose in two studies, study #8 without placebo).

interpretation_gap.note: Quoted abstract phrase is exact. The causal Discussion readings and the untested preparation and dose-sequence speculation are correctly flagged and not reproduced.

missed: Implication of key finding 3 not drawn: by the Results text (4th paragraph) pre-drug well-being was significantly associated with every subjective scale except VAS bad drug effect, changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood, which includes 5D-ASC anxious ego dissolution and anxiety, and the Discussion (1st paragraph) says effects were more pronounced with higher well-being and also with higher pre-drug anxiety. So in these data a better mood went with stronger effects generally, including anxiety-type scales, rather than with a less challenging session (sign for those scales is in Fig. 1, not viewable). Claims using Vizeli as support for 'better state of mind, less challenging experience' should say so.

Discussion, 7th paragraph: 'although all but one of the analyzed studies included a placebo session' is a second place where the paper itself states the 8/9 fact, worth adding to reporting issue 1's locator.
